title: Google launches Gemini 4 Neon with a 1M-token context and $3 input pricing
summary: If you regularly process large batches of spreadsheets, PDFs, and charts in one go and find big models slow and token-hungry, Gemini 4 Neon is built for exactly that: a 1M-token context that handles those inputs at a cost well below the big models.
ai_summary: On November 18 Google launched Gemini 4 Neon: cheaper than Carbon and able to handle more complex work than Hydrogen. It has a 1M-token context, $3 per million input tokens, $15 per million output tokens, and $0.15 per million cached input tokens. It scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at xhigh, ranking #3 overall, and ranks #2 on the Vals Index with 70.9%. At the default high thinking level, it costs 32% less per task than Carbon. It is live today in the Gemini API, AI Studio, Gemini for business, and Google Antigravity. Caveat: many of these results come from vendor or third-party benchmarks and need validation on your own workloads.
brief: Input costs $3 per million tokens, output $15 per million tokens, and cached input $0.15 per million tokens (a 95% discount), with a 1M-token context.
Scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at xhigh, #3 overall, and 70.9% on the Vals Index, #2.
Default high thinking level costs 32% less per task than Carbon; CWE-bench v2 scores 70.7%, 3.4 percentage points above Carbon.
Live today in the Gemini API, AI Studio, Gemini for business, and Google Antigravity; Pro/Ultra subscribers can also choose it in the Gemini app.

blocks.p: Gemini 4 Neon is a new model in Google's Gemini 4 family, announced on November 18. Google splits the family into three tiers: Carbon handles the hardest, longest projects; Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution; and Neon sits in between—close to frontier reasoning, but faster and less token-hungry.

It is built for complex software engineering, knowledge work, and scientific workflows completed end-to-end at speed. These tasks often involve spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video at once; Neon can process all of them in a single 1M-token context and return structured output.

Rollout started on launch day: developers can access it through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio; enterprises through Gemini for business (API or model dropdown); Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can select it in Google Antigravity and the Gemini app. For cybersecurity, a version for trusted defenders will open through the Fairwind Program in the coming days.

sections.h: Pricing and context: how much it costs and how much it can hold

blocks.p: Pricing is direct: $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Cached input is cheapest at $0.15 per million tokens—a 95% discount—for the part of a repeated large context that hits the cache, such as always sending the same long document.

The context window is 1M tokens, enough for one request to hold several long PDFs, a large spreadsheet, and a few audio or video clips, so the model can synthesize across files in the same material instead of splitting the work into several calls.

sections.h: How to read the benchmarks: intelligence, enterprise, and agents

blocks.p: Google cites a range of third-party benchmarks. We'll focus on three categories, with one caveat up front: these scores come from specific evaluation sets, and they don't guarantee the same results on your tasks.

General intelligence: On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite intelligence benchmark, Neon scores 61 at the highest xhigh setting and ranks #3 overall, behind several larger, slower models. Note this is the top setting; the everyday default is lower but cheaper.

Enterprise capability: It scores 70.9% on the Vals Index and ranks #2, landing on the Pareto frontier—meaning at the same cost, there is basically no clearly better option. It also ranks #1 on the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench, and #1 on most Surge AI benchmarks covering finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following.

Automation agents: Zapier's AutomationBench scores 56.3%, #1. Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 returns $16,843, #1—it simulates running a business long-term, and higher is better. Arena's Agent Arena Index, based on real agent sessions, gives Neon 1,336 points and #2 globally across more than 4,200 sessions.
Science and math: Terminal-Bench Science 70.5%, RiemannBench 84.0%, HLE-Diamond 71.3%; Google describes these as best in class.

sections.h: Coding and long tasks: why it's built for production

blocks.p: Neon's focus isn't writing a small function; it's running long, tool-heavy agent workflows. Google stresses that Neon compresses context reliably in long sessions, avoids re-reading the same files, and reports progress as it works.
On coding leaderboards: Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index 58.6, #1; Terminal-Bench 4.1 65.2%; FrontierCode 2.0 46.2% at the default high setting.

The most interesting result is SWE-sweep: the mini-SWE harness alone scores only 12.8%, but in Google Antigravity it rises to 39.0%. Google says this shows how much the Antigravity harness can unlock—in other words, scores are highly sensitive to environment setup, so don't treat a bare-harness score as the ceiling.
In Google Antigravity, Neon can also act as an Orchestrator, directing parallel Hydrogen subagents.

sections.h: Four thinking levels: the token-saving dial

blocks.p: Neon has four thinking levels, so teams can tune it to the task—from a token-saving fast mode up to the highest setting, xhigh. The default is high.

At the default high setting, its intelligence index score remains high but costs 32% less per task than Carbon. On both the Vals and Agent Arena benchmarks, high sits on the Pareto frontier and costs roughly 50% to 80% less per task than top competing frontier models.
xhigh adds deeper multi-step reasoning and gives the highest intelligence score, while still costing 36%+ less than competitors at their highest settings.
These 'cheaper by X%' figures are Google's own framing, based on specific benchmark cost calculations; your workflow may not see the same savings.

callout.title: Watch the measurement caveats
callout.text: For the 50%–80% and 36%+ savings, Google doesn't say which competitors or which tasks were used, so treat them as directional.

sections.h: Safety and cybersecurity: secure code, vulnerability hunting, injection defense

blocks.p: Safety is its own focus area for Neon, with the goal of finding, validating, and fixing vulnerabilities quickly and cheaply.

list: AutoBaxBench: generates more secure code than Carbon across easy, medium, and hard tiers; 76% on the hard tier, state-of-the-art.
WebExploitBench v1.2: penetration testing, 51.26%, state-of-the-art, at about half the cost of competing large models.
SEC-bench Pro: finds code vulnerabilities, 90.5%, state-of-the-art, at about half the cost per challenge.
ExploitGym: validates risk at frontier level, using half the tokens of Carbon.
CWE-bench v2: patches vulnerabilities at 70.7%, 3.4 percentage points above Carbon.

blocks.p: The safety stack also monitors agent behavior itself. On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark with real-time safeguards at the highest setting, malicious prompt injection attacks planted in web pages, emails, and documents had a 0.0% success rate. The agent honesty evaluation passed 99.2%, and the coding cheating evaluation showed a 2.45% shortcut rate—the lowest in the Gemini 4 family.
The version for trusted defenders is called Gemini 4 Neon for cyber, opening through the Fairwind Program in the coming days; request access through your Cloud account manager.

sections.h: What you can build: three official demos

blocks.p: Google shows several demos in Google Antigravity, making the point that Neon can take an idea all the way to a finished product, not just a single response.

fig.title: One image becomes a 100,000-cell spreadsheet

panels.title: 100,000-cell Google Sheet
panels.text: Over 500,000 live formulas, no embedded images, no Apps Script

blocks.p: Another demo is a first-person WebGL2 ski simulator: real Mont Blanc and Chamonix terrain, 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics, six alpine runs, and no pre-made assets.

Another uses /swarm to rebuild Alan Turing's 1936 study at King's College, Cambridge from archival photos: from King's Chapel outside to Room X.8, in interactive 3D, with a working Universal Turing Machine on the desk.

Free allowances and how many tokens are included in subscription plans.

blocks.p: The value: one model that covers complex coding, business analysis, and scientific reasoning at a lower price than large models, while reading fewer files and compressing context reliably in long tasks.

The trade-off: many of the '#1' and 'half price' claims come from Google's own framing or specific benchmarks, so you need to revalidate them on your own production data. It's also a paid model, requiring a subscription or API billing.

list: If you do legal, tax, or financial spreadsheet automation in an enterprise, Neon stands out on the relevant benchmarks and is worth testing on real data.
If you're a developer running long agent tasks and care about SWE-sweep rising from 12.8% to 39.0% in Antigravity, set up a similar environment before evaluating.
If you're on a security team, contact your Cloud account manager to request the Fairwind Program.
If you're an individual user, you need a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription to select Neon in the Gemini app.

sources.note: All data comes from this one Google blog post. Schematic figures (thinking levels, single-image-to-spreadsheet, Neon orchestrating subagents) are drawn from the descriptions in the post; level names and cell counts are illustrative.
